newsitem.title: USA: Coffee prices soar before Colombia strikes.
newsitem.headline: Coffee prices soar before Colombia strikes.

text.p: Coffee futures rocketed to a 20-month high Monday as a pending labor strike in Colombia threatened coffee exports from the world's second-largest producer.
The strike by more than 800,000 Colombian government workers, due to begin at midnight Monday, would be the largest in 20 years, according to labor leaders there.

In other markets, wheat futures prices tumbled to a 20-month low on heavy selling ahead of Wednesday's Agriculture Department crop report. Heating oil prices rose, while frozen concentrated orange juice prices fell.
Coffee futures at New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange shot to a 20-month high due to bullish technical factors and the Colombia strike.
Traders and analysts said a strike might interrupt the flow of coffee while inventories are extremely low.
"It is still a tight situation, and any reports on short-term disruptions is viewed as bullish," said Dean Witter analyst Steve Platt.
Also a concern was a drop last month in Colombia's production, said Merrill Lynch analyst Judith Ganes.
On Friday, Colombia's National Coffee Growers' Federation said the country's January production fell to 778,000 132-pound bags compared with 2.08 million bags in January 1996.
"There is the potential for a small Colombia crop based on the production data," said Ganes. "778,000 bags is the lowest level during January in eight years."
March coffee futures surged to a life-of-contract high of 159.75 cents per pound before closing at 158.65 cents, up 7.60 cents a pound.
At the Chicago Board of Trade March soft red winter wheat futures fell to a contract low and the lowest close since May 1995.

The market underwent a downward shift before the release Wednesday of the Agriculture Department's supply-demand report, the traders said. Analysts said they did not expect the department to make much of a change in the wheat balance sheets.
But, grain traders have been bearish on wheat lately because the high price of U.S. wheat has turned export customers to lower-priced, foreign-grown wheat.
March soft red winter wheat futures closed 3-1/2 cents lower at $3.52-1/2 per bushel.

Frozen concentrated orange juice futures settled down sharply for the second straight session at New York's Cotton Exchange on selling ahead of the Agriculture Department's Florida crop estimate and forecasts for mild weather in Florida.
Analysts expect the agency to estimate the crop at 205 million to 210 million 90-pound boxes, down from the previous crop estimate of a record 220 million boxes.
The estimate is the first official department tally of the crop since a Jan. 19 freeze.
Also undermining the market were forecasts for warm weather across the Florida citrus belt for the next 10 days.
Most-active March futures fell 2.65 cents to 80.65 cents per pound.
New York Mercantile Exchange heating oil prices rose sharply Monday on tight supplies in the Gulf of Mexico, which prompted late buying in crude oil and gasoline.

Spot market traders said there were tighter supplies of heating oil in Texas because refiners have shifted their output away from distillates, which include heating oil and diesel, to gasoline ahead of the summer driving season.
NYMEX March heating oil settled up 1.23 cents at 61.76 cents a gallon. March crude ended up 23 cents at $22.46 a barrel, while March gasoline finished up 0.47 cent a gallon at 63.53 cents.
